chapters.title: The Price of a Lie — Emotional and Psychological Impact

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: Betrayal Trauma and the Emotional Cost of Deception
assets.visual_frame_description: A 4-stage emotional spiral diagram: Stage 1 (Discovery) — shock, numbness, physical collapse. Stage 2 (Processing) — anger, rage, desire for revenge. Stage 3 (Grieving) — sadness, self-blame, questioning reality. Stage 4 (Healing) — acceptance, learning, empowerment through knowledge.
assets.player_mission: Analyze 12 betrayal scenarios. For each, identify the stage of emotional response, the specific emotions present, and recommend appropriate support strategies.
key_concepts: Discovering a lie from someone you trust triggers shock, depression, numbness, and rage
The closer the relationship, the more devastating the betrayal
Betrayal trauma is a recognized psychological wound that can shatter a person’s worldview
Feeling betrayed can turn calm, rational people into violent criminals (Clara Harris case)
Financial betrayal (Madoff) can be as devastating as romantic betrayal
The betrayed person often blames themselves: Why didn’t I see the signs?
Chronic lying destroys self-esteem and creates hypervigilance
Recovery from betrayal requires: accepting the reality, processing anger, rebuilding trust selectively
Glass argues that understanding body language clues empowers victims and prevents future betrayal
The catharsis of discovery — finding the truth, no matter how painful, is ultimately healthier than living in deception

chapters.title: The Evolution of a Liar — Animals, Children, and Teens

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: Lying Across Development: From Animal Deception to Adolescent Lies
assets.visual_frame_description: A developmental timeline: Age 0-2 (pre-lie, no theory of mind), Age 2-3 (first lies emerge, obvious), Age 4-5 (better concealment, simple deception), Age 6-12 (social lies develop), Age 13-16 (peak lying frequency, complex deceptions), Age 17+ (declining lies, mature understanding). Animal examples shown at each stage.
assets.player_mission: Analyze 12 child/teen lying scenarios. For each, determine the developmental stage, the lie type (typical vs. concerning), and recommend the appropriate parental response.
key_concepts: Deception is found throughout the animal kingdom: camouflage, mimicry, bluffing, and hiding
Animals deceive for survival: predators hide, prey feign death, some species mimic others
Children begin lying around age 2-3 once they develop theory of mind
Young children’s lies are transparent (no attempt to conceal nonverbal leakage)
By age 4-5, children become better liars as cognitive skills develop
Teens lie more frequently: about social lives, activities, and to assert independence
The most common teen lies: who they’re with, what they’re doing, homework completion
Excessive lying in children may signal underlying issues (anxiety, attention-seeking, or modeling parental behavior)
Parental response to child lying matters: harsh punishment increases lying skill; discussion about honesty reduces it
Adolescent lying peaks around ages 14-16 then declines as maturity develops
Some lying in childhood/teens is a normal developmental milestone, not a character flaw

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: The Seven Core Motives for Adult Deception
assets.visual_frame_description: A 7-panel display showing each lying motive with a representative scenario: Panel 1 (Avoid Punishment) — child with broken vase. Panel 2 (Gain Advantage) — inflated resume. Panel 3 (Protect Others) — surprise party denial. Panel 4 (Self-Protection) — hiding a mistake. Panel 5 (Impress) — exaggerated story. Panel 6 (Avoid Conflict) — I love your cooking. Panel 7 (Habit) — compulsive bragging.
assets.player_mission: Analyze 16 adult lies and identify the primary motive behind each. Some lies have multiple motives — identify the dominant one. Different motives produce different behavioral tell patterns.
key_concepts: Glass identifies 7 primary reasons adults lie: to avoid punishment, to gain advantage, to protect others, to protect self, to impress, to avoid conflict, and habit
Avoiding punishment: the most common motive — I didn’t do it
Gaining advantage: financial gain, career advancement, romantic conquest
Protecting others: the white lie to spare feelings, protect reputation, or shield from harm
Self-protection: lying to avoid embarrassment, shame, or vulnerability
Impressing others: exaggeration, name-dropping, embellishment of accomplishments
Conflict avoidance: agreeing to avoid arguments, pretending to like something, withholding disagreement
Habitual lying: some people lie so often it becomes automatic — they may not even realize they are lying
Pathological lying: compulsive, without clear benefit, often grandiose — may indicate underlying psychological issues
Understanding the motive behind a lie is key to catching it — different motives produce different behavioral clues
Fear-of-punishment lies show different body language than impression-management lies
The same behavior can be a lie for one reason and truth for another — context is everything

Financial scams: phishing, Nigerian prince, romance scams, fake charities
Written communication red flags: inconsistency, vague details, reluctance to video chat, avoiding specific questions

Trust your gut online — if something feels off, it probably is

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: Body-Wide Deception Signals: From Head to Toe
assets.visual_frame_description: A full-body heat map showing deception clue zones: Head (tilts, shakes), Eyes (blink changes, blocking), Nose (touch), Mouth (press, fake smile), Jaw (clench), Neck (touch, swallow), Shoulders (shrug reduction), Arms (cross, barrier), Hands (face touch, freeze), Torso (lean away), Legs (bounce, interlock), Feet (point to exit, tap). Each zone has intensity indicators.
assets.player_mission: Analyze 20 video clips of people potentially lying. Scan each body zone for deception clues. Identify all present clues across channels. Determine whether the cluster of clues indicates deception or another cause (stress, discomfort, habit, cold room).
key_concepts: Head: tilting away signals discomfort, shaking no while saying yes is a contradiction clue
Eyes: excessive blinking or no blinking (staring), looking away at key moments, eye blocking (rubbing eyes)
Nose: touching or rubbing the nose increases during deception (blood flow changes make it tingle)
Mouth: lip pressing, lip biting, fake smiles (non-Duchenne, no eye involvement), lip licking (dry mouth response)
Jaw: clenching signals suppressed anger or frustration at being caught
Ears: touching, pulling, or rubbing ears increases with discomfort
Skin: flushing (anger/embarrassment) or paling (fear)
Arms: crossed arms, reduced gesturing (cognitive load), holding objects as barrier
Hands: decreased palm exposure, hand wringing, fidgeting, hand-to-face touching, frozen hands
Torso: leaning away, turning body toward exit, shallow breathing
Legs and feet: pointing toward exit, foot tapping/bouncing, interlocking legs, ankle lock
Posture: rigid, frozen posture signals high cognitive load (trying to control all channels)
Glass provides celebrity photo analysis showing specific tells at the moment of deception
No single body part is diagnostic — clusters of behaviors across multiple channels are reliable

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: Facial Tells: Micro-Expressions, Asymmetry, and False Smiles
assets.visual_frame_description: A close-up face dissection showing: micro-expression zones (fear brows, contempt lip curl, anger eye narrowing), asymmetry indicators (left-right comparison), Duchenne vs. non-Duchenne smile comparisons, timing graphs (smooth vs. abrupt onset/offset), and the frozen face warning zone.
assets.player_mission: Identify 20 facial expressions and classify each as: genuine, micro-expression, masked, falsified, or neutral. Use FACS-style analysis: check symmetry, timing, muscle involvement (especially AU6 for smiles), and context congruence.
key_concepts: The face is the most expressive but also the most controllable part of the body — liars work hardest to control it
Micro-expressions: full emotions flashing in 1/25 - 1/5 second, revealing concealed feelings
Common micro-expressions during deception: fear (of being caught), contempt (for the victim), anger (at being questioned), disgust (at the situation)
Macro-expression suppression: cutting off an expression before it fully forms
Asymmetry: genuine expressions are symmetrical; falsified expressions may be stronger on one side
Eye contact myths: liars do NOT necessarily avoid eye contact — many make MORE eye contact to appear honest
Fake smiles: non-Duchenne (no crow’s feet, no cheek raising, held too long or too short)
Mismatched expressions: verbal content doesn’t match facial expression (e.g., I’m fine with furrowed brows)
Frozen face: suppressing ALL facial movement — creates an unnatural, wooden appearance
Vocal-facial mismatch: pleasant tone with angry micro-expression
Glass emphasizes looking for the flash — a brief true expression before the social mask returns

assets.visual_frame_description: A voice spectrogram comparison: truthful speech shows natural pitch variation, moderate rate, smooth flow. key_concepts: Vocal pitch rises under stress — liars often have higher-pitched voices when being deceptive
Pitch variation decreases — liars sound flat or monotone as they focus on controlling their story
Speech rate: can increase (nervous energy) or decrease (cognitive load, thinking hard)
Pauses: longer pauses before answering, more filled pauses (um, uh, like), hesitation at key points
Volume: may increase (defensive, angry) or decrease (withdrawn, trying not to be heard)
Voice tremors/quivering signals intense emotion — could be fear of being caught or genuine distress
Clearing throat indicates stress and dry mouth response
Stuttering or speech errors (repetitions, false starts) increase under cognitive load
Vocal tone becomes harsh or clipped when anger is present
Predictable phrasing: liars may repeat questions before answering (buying time) or use the same phrases repeatedly (rehearsed narrative)
Overspecificity: too many irrelevant details that make the story too perfect
Reluctance to elaborate: short answers to questions that deserve longer responses
The voice, like the feet, is harder to control than the face — it reveals more than the liar intends

assets.topic: Cue Scrubber: Word Choice, Phrasing, and Linguistic Red Flags
assets.visual_frame_description: A speech analysis dashboard: transcript of a liar vs. truth-teller side by side. Deceptive transcript is highlighted: pronoun distancing (no I), negative language (red), qualifier flags (to be honest), vagueness (faded text), time/sequence markers. Truthful transcript: rich with I, spontaneous corrections, sensory details, emotional language, natural timeline.
assets.player_mission: Analyze 16 transcripts of people being interviewed. For each, identify the linguistic red flags present. Determine whether the speaker is being truthful or deceptive based on speech content analysis alone.
key_concepts: Pronoun distancing: liars use fewer I statements — that happened not I did that
Negative language: more no, never, didn’t, not — liars protest too much
Overly formal language: liars use more formal, stilted speech compared to their normal casual style
Specific denials: I did NOT have sexual relations with that woman (Clinton) — over-precise denial
Qualifiers: to be honest, frankly, truthfully, I swear — these often precede lies
Vagueness: lack of specific details, sensory information (what you saw, heard, smelled)
Time/sequence issues: liars avoid chronological order (harder to maintain) or tell events in perfect chronological sequence (rehearsed)
Missing emotions: liars don’t describe their emotional state during the event — they narrate facts without feelings
Irrelevant details: too many unnecessary specifics to make the story sound true
Questions repeated before answering: What was I doing on Tuesday at 3pm? Let me think... — buying time
Defensiveness: attacking the questioner instead of answering (Why would you even ask that?)
Scripted language: repeated phrases that sound rehearsed, not spontaneous
Lack of spontaneous correction: truthful people correct themselves; liars stick rigidly to their story
Self-reference: liars may refer to themselves in third person (a person in my position would never...)
